case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal district court that had original jurisdiction when it filed and then stayed a case pending arbitration under the FAA retains jurisdiction to decide post-arbitration motions (e.g., confirmation/vacatur) within the same stayed case without identifying a new, independent basis for federal jurisdiction.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Arbitration Act, 9 U.S.C. §§ 1–16 (especially §§ 9–10 regarding confirmation/vacatur, and the FAA’s jurisdictional framework as construed in Supreme Court precedent).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that once a federal court properly has original jurisdiction and stays the action pending arbitration, it retains jurisdiction in that same ongoing case to resolve post-arbitration motions (confirm/vacate/modify) without forcing the parties to establish a second, redundant jurisdictional hook. Petitioner maintains that multiple circuits treat the stayed action as continuing and allow the court to proceed to post-arbitration relief, and that requiring a new jurisdictional showing is doctrinally wrong and creates inefficiency and potential forum-shopping.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that the Second Circuit correctly required an independent jurisdictional basis for post-arbitration motions under the FAA, emphasizing that the FAA itself does not confer federal jurisdiction and that post-arbitration requests (confirmation/vacatur) must satisfy federal jurisdiction requirements on their own. They also contend the circuit split is weak/underdeveloped and that this case is a poor vehicle due to asserted factual/procedural wrinkles (including alternative arguments made below), so Supreme Court review is premature.
key_precedents: Union No. 2 United Ass’n of Journeymen v. Bleecker, 841 F.2d 461 (2d Cir. 1988)
Beijing Shougang Mining Inv. Co. v. Mongolia, 11 F.4th 144 (2d Cir. 2021)
Smarter Tools Inc. v. Chongqing SENCI Imp. & Exp. Trade Co., 57 F.4th 372 (2d Cir. 2023)
Weiss v. Sallie Mae, Inc., 939 F.3d 105 (2d Cir. 2019)
Triestman v. Fed. Bureau of Prisons, 470 F.3d 471 (2d Cir. 2006)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Alito press the strongest objection: Badgerow treats §§ 9–10 as distinct “applications” requiring an independent jurisdictional basis, and Kokkonen warns that docket posture cannot manufacture jurisdiction. But that critique assumes the post-award filing is a new civil action; where the district court had undisputed § 1331 jurisdiction at the outset and entered a mandatory § 3 stay rather than dismissing, nothing in Chapter 1 clearly strips subject-matter jurisdiction midstream or renders the still-pending case a nullity. The sound, text-respecting line is to confine Badgerow to freestanding, first-in-time post-award petitions and to allow award-related relief within the same stayed action the court already had power to adjudicate. Given the forum uncertainty and duplicative-proceedings trap Respondent’s rule would create, it is necessary and prudent to decide that jurisdiction persists to conclude the pending case—without treating the FAA as an independent jurisdictional grant.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice argue that a § 3 stay preserves the original § 1331 “case,” so the court may later resolve §§ 9–10 motions without a new jurisdictional showing. But that treats docket continuity as a jurisdictional grant, which Badgerow rejects by requiring an independent basis for the distinct statutory “application” to confirm or vacate, and which Kokkonen cautions cannot be supplied by ancillary or case-management notions. The FAA’s structure reinforces the point: where Congress wanted to confer federal jurisdiction for arbitration-related enforcement (e.g., Chapter 2; § 8), it did so expressly, and Chapter 1 contains no comparable authorization to adjudicate post-award relief merely because a merits case was once properly filed and stayed. Workability concerns, however real, cannot justify expanding federal jurisdiction beyond what the statute confers, especially when the supposed “midstream reset” is simply adherence to Congress’s limited jurisdictional grants at each distinct step.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that a § 3 stay leaves a § 1331 case pending, so the court is merely “finishing the job” in the same docket. But that conflates docket-continuation with jurisdiction-continuation for a distinct statutory “application” under §§ 9–10, and Badgerow treats those post-award applications as requiring an independent jurisdictional basis on their face—precisely to avoid letting posture do the work of a jurisdictional grant. As Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas emphasize, allowing a stayed merits action to serve as a jurisdictional anchor would recreate, through procedural happenstance, the sort of jurisdictional expansion Badgerow rejected, and Kokkonen cautions that ancillary or procedural labels cannot supply subject-matter jurisdiction Congress has not conferred. Whatever the workability concerns Justice Kavanaugh raises, they cannot justify reading into Chapter 1 a midstream authorization to adjudicate §§ 9–10 relief absent an independent jurisdictional basis.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that a § 3 stay preserves a still-pending § 1331 case, so a post-award motion looks like merely finishing the same dispute without any “midstream” loss of jurisdiction. But as Justice Barrett and Justice Alito stress, Badgerow treats §§ 9–10 as jurisdictionally distinct applications, and Kokkonen cautions that procedural posture cannot supply subject-matter jurisdiction for a different kind of relief Congress did not affirmatively place within federal courts’ limited grants. If we let the stayed merits action serve as a jurisdictional anchor, we effectively recreate—through docket happenstance—the very bootstrapping Badgerow rejected, with downstream complexity that will predictably burden less-resourced parties forced to navigate shifting forums and uncertain enforcement pathways. The practical inefficiencies Petitioners identify are real, but absent clearer text, I cannot endorse an atextual expansion of federal jurisdiction; that remedy is for Congress.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Alito’s strongest point—rooted in Badgerow and Kokkonen—is that docket posture cannot supply jurisdiction for a statutorily distinct §§ 9–10 “application.” But that framing assumes the court is being asked to entertain a new civil action; here, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, § 1331 jurisdiction indisputably attached to an ongoing case, and § 3’s mandatory stay keeps that case pending rather than extinguished. Reading Badgerow to require a midstream jurisdictional “reset” after arbitration would create an arbitration-specific divestiture rule that Chapter 1 nowhere states, while producing the workability and forum-shopping problems Justice Kavanaugh identifies, all without actually enlarging federal jurisdiction beyond the original grant. Kokkonen’s caution is satisfied because we are not manufacturing jurisdiction from an “ancillary” label; we are exercising continuing authority to conclude a properly filed federal action on the same docket.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Alito rightly stress Badgerow’s requirement of an independent jurisdictional basis for a freestanding §§ 9–10 “application,” and Kokkonen’s warning that labels like “ancillary” cannot conjure jurisdiction. But that objection assumes the post-award filing is a new civil action rather than a motion in a still-pending case the court indisputably possessed § 1331 jurisdiction to hear and that § 3 says the court “shall” stay—not dismiss—pending arbitration. Nothing in the FAA’s text supplies a midstream jurisdictional divestiture rule, and I am reluctant to invent an arbitration-specific jurisdictional reset that Congress did not enact. As the Chief Justice notes, confining Badgerow to first-in-time, stand-alone post-award petitions respects its holding without treating a stayed federal case as jurisdictionally dead until refiled elsewhere.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Alito’s strongest point—drawing on Badgerow and Kokkonen—is that §§ 9–10 are distinct “applications” and that docket posture cannot manufacture jurisdiction Congress did not confer. But that objection has its greatest force when the federal court is being asked to entertain a freestanding post-award filing as a new matter; here, as the Chief Justice stresses, the court already had undisputed § 1331 jurisdiction over a still-pending civil action that § 3 required it to stay, and nothing in Chapter 1 clearly compels a midstream jurisdictional reset or treats the stayed case as jurisdictionally dead. Recognizing authority to confirm/vacate within that same stayed action does not create jurisdiction “out of thin air”; it uses the existing jurisdiction to bring the already-proper case to judgment, and Badgerow can be read narrowly to govern first-in-time, stand-alone petitions without rewriting the stayed-case posture. Practical workability reinforces that reading, because Respondent’s rule would predictably force duplicative state-court proceedings and incentivize strategic dismissal-versus-stay maneuvering without a clear statutory command.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kagan press the best point for Petitioner: a § 3 stay keeps the federal civil action pending, so a post-award request can be framed as simply finishing the same case rather than initiating a new one. But that framing cannot overcome Badgerow’s insistence that §§ 9–10 proceedings are statutory “applications” requiring an independent jurisdictional basis on their face; otherwise, the stayed merits suit becomes a jurisdictional anchor that functionally recreates the look-through expansion Badgerow rejected. As Justice Alito notes via Kokkonen, docket posture and case-management authority do not supply subject-matter jurisdiction for distinct relief Congress treated separately, and nothing in Chapter 1 supplies the missing grant—particularly given the FAA’s structure and the presence of express jurisdictional provisions elsewhere, as Justice Thomas emphasizes. Workability concerns are serious, but they do not justify short-circuiting a hard jurisdictional limit through an atextual ancillary-jurisdiction theory tied to whether the court stayed rather than dismissed.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Alito rightly press that Badgerow and Kokkonen forbid treating procedural labels as jurisdictional alchemy, and that §§ 9–10 relief must rest on a valid jurisdictional footing. But in the § 3 stay posture, that footing was supplied at the outset by an undisputed § 1331 civil action that remains pending; nothing in Chapter 1 textually commands a midstream “jurisdictional reset” or converts the stayed case into a nullity such that the court suddenly lacks power to bring the same action to judgment. As the Chief Justice frames it, Badgerow answers how to assess jurisdiction for a freestanding, first-in-time post-award filing—not whether a federal court loses authority to resolve award-related motions filed in the very case it was required to stay. Treating confirmation/vacatur as a continuation within the same pending action cabins Badgerow’s no-look-through rule without creating an arbitration-specific divestiture principle that would spill over to other interlocutory postures.

John Roberts.reasoning: We have an independent obligation to assure ourselves of jurisdiction, and here the district court indisputably possessed original subject-matter jurisdiction at the outset (e.g., a federal-question Title VII action) and entered a § 3 stay rather than dismissing—so the case remained the same live civil action on the court’s docket. The FAA’s §§ 9–10 do not themselves confer jurisdiction, but that principle (as in Badgerow) addresses stand-alone confirmation/vacatur applications; it does not strip a court of subject-matter jurisdiction it already has over a pending, stayed federal case or require parties to manufacture a second jurisdictional “hook” to obtain post-arbitration relief in that same action. Treating the post-arbitration motion as a continuation of the existing case avoids the very forum uncertainty that makes it necessary and prudent to decide the jurisdictional question now, while remaining faithful to the distinction between limits on FAA remedial authority and true subject-matter jurisdiction. Because Badgerow’s no-look-through rule governs only when jurisdiction must be found on the face of a new §§ 9–10 application, it does not compel dismissal where the district court is simply exercising continuing jurisdiction in an already-properly-filed and stayed federal action.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under first principles, a federal court’s power depends on a valid statutory grant of subject-matter jurisdiction, and the FAA’s §§9–10 supply procedures but “do not themselves confer federal jurisdiction.” The fact that the district court initially had original jurisdiction to entertain the underlying civil action and entered a §3 stay does not expand the court’s jurisdictional grant to encompass later, distinct applications to confirm or vacate an award; absent a clear congressional authorization to “retain” jurisdiction (as in FAA §8), the court must identify an independent jurisdictional basis for the post-award application on its face. Reading the FAA as an integrated scheme, Congress provided specific jurisdictional rules where it intended (e.g., Chapter 2’s §§203–206), and its silence in Chapter 1 confirms that post-award relief is not jurisdictionally automatic simply because an earlier case remains stayed. Because petitioner seeks post-arbitration relief without establishing an independent federal jurisdictional hook for the §§9–10 application, the district court lacked power to decide it.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The antecedent question is whether the district court’s decision to stay (rather than dismiss) left it with procedural authority to manage the case; but that does not answer the separate, downstream question whether the court has subject-matter jurisdiction to adjudicate a post-award FAA § 9/§ 10 application. Under Badgerow, a confirmation/vacatur request must itself show an independent jurisdictional basis on its face, and the FAA’s post-award provisions do not supply one. Nor can the existence of the earlier stayed federal action be treated as a jurisdiction-conferring device—procedural mechanisms and case-management posture cannot manufacture jurisdiction where it is otherwise absent, consistent with Kokkonen’s principle that rules of procedure cannot create federal jurisdiction. Because the parties are nondiverse and the § 9/§ 10 applications rest only on the federal character of the arbitrated dispute, the district court lacked jurisdiction to decide the post-award motions in the stayed case.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Because the FAA does not itself confer federal jurisdiction, a district court’s post-arbitration power to confirm or vacate an award must rest on a jurisdictional basis that exists for the § 9–10 application itself, not merely on the fact that the court once had jurisdiction over a now-stayed merits action. A § 3 stay preserves the court’s ability to adjudicate the claims that supplied original jurisdiction if arbitration fails or does not resolve them, but it does not enlarge federal jurisdiction to reach a different species of proceeding—confirmation/vacatur—that Badgerow treats as jurisdictionally separate and textually distinct from § 4. While I am attentive to the practical burdens this rule can impose—especially on workers, consumers, and civil-rights plaintiffs forced into arbitration—those real-world harms cannot justify stretching Article III and Congress’s carefully limited jurisdictional grants beyond their terms. The fairer, more durable solution is for Congress to provide a clear remedial path in federal court for enforcement and review of arbitration awards where vulnerable parties are most at risk, rather than for courts to create an atextual “jurisdictional-anchor” doctrine.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: A district court that properly possessed original jurisdiction over the filed action and entered a § 3 stay retains authority to finish that same case, including by resolving the post-arbitration motions that determine whether the arbitration has in fact settled the parties’ dispute and what judgment (if any) should enter. Nothing in §§ 9–10 suggests Congress meant to require a duplicative, second-round jurisdictional showing for motions that are part and parcel of administering the stayed federal action; reading the statute that way would be textually unmoored and badly unworkable, inviting needless new filings and forum-shopping. And to the extent one thinks an additional jurisdictional label is needed, the post-arbitration motions are at minimum sufficiently tied to the original action to fall within the court’s continuing/supplemental (or ancillary) authority to manage and conclude proceedings already within its jurisdiction. That approach preserves the FAA’s non-jurisdiction-conferring rule while providing a coherent, administrable framework for courts supervising stayed cases.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The district court indisputably possessed original jurisdiction over the parties’ civil action when it was filed, and a stay under FAA § 3 is not a jurisdiction-stripping act—it suspends merits proceedings while leaving the case pending on the court’s docket. Nothing in the FAA’s text says that jurisdiction evaporates upon completion of arbitration or that a party must supply a second, duplicative jurisdictional hook to obtain the statutorily contemplated post-arbitration relief in the same ongoing case; imposing that extra requirement would be a judge-made hurdle untethered to enacted language. Badgerow’s holding that FAA §§ 9–10 do not themselves confer jurisdiction answers a different question—whether an independent, freestanding post-award application filed for the first time in federal court may proceed—and it does not defeat a federal court’s continuing (ancillary) authority to resolve award-related motions that are part of the still-live, stayed action. Article III presents no mootness problem because the dispute has continuing real-world effect (whether the award will be confirmed or vacated), and allowing strategic relabeling to force a new jurisdictional showing would elevate form over substance.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Because the district court indisputably possessed Article III subject-matter jurisdiction at the outset and then entered a § 3 stay rather than dismissing the action, the case remained on the federal docket and the court retained authority to resolve matters necessary to effectuate that existing jurisdiction in a workable way—including post-arbitration confirmation or vacatur in the same stayed proceeding. Badgerow correctly holds that the FAA does not itself supply jurisdiction and rejects “look-through” for stand-alone §§ 9–10 applications, but it did not address—and should not be extended to undermine—traditional ancillary jurisdiction and the settled understanding that a stay preserves the court’s continuing control of the case. History, practice, and workability favor allowing the same court that compelled or stayed for arbitration to finish the job without forcing a redundant new jurisdictional showing that invites inefficiency and forum-shopping. That approach respects precedent while avoiding a novel, formalistic jurisdictional trap that Congress did not clearly require in the FAA’s stay framework.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: I would start with the jurisdictional question, because Article III and the governing jurisdictional statutes limit what a federal court may do at each procedural stage. Under Badgerow’s text-and-structure reading of FAA §§ 9–10, an application to confirm or vacate is jurisdictionally distinct and must rest on an independent jurisdictional basis apparent on the face of that application; the FAA supplies the mechanism but not the power. Treating a previously stayed § 3 action as a freestanding “jurisdictional anchor” for later §§ 9–10 relief would create a mismatch in the FAA’s scheme—effectively expanding federal enforcement jurisdiction for awards in a way Badgerow rejected—and would invite courts to short-circuit a hard jurisdictional limit by procedural happenstance. Because the record here shows the post-arbitration confirmation/vacatur request was not supported by its own federal-question or diversity basis (and the FAA alone cannot do the work), the district court lacked jurisdiction to decide it.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Once the district court properly exercised undisputed original jurisdiction over the filed action, a stay pending arbitration did not terminate that case or divest the court of authority to resolve the next, tightly connected “aspect” of the same matter—post-arbitration relief concerning the award—so long as it proceeds within the stayed docket rather than as a new, freestanding FAA petition. Badgerow and Vaden restrict when the FAA can supply (or expand) original jurisdiction in standalone applications, but they do not compel a judge-made rule that a court loses jurisdiction midstream and must demand a second, redundant jurisdictional hook after arbitration concludes. Traditional baseline principles favor treating the post-arbitration confirmation/vacatur motion as part of the same ongoing case management continuum that the court stayed, and nothing in the FAA’s text requires the categorical, arbitration-specific jurisdictional forfeiture that Respondents propose. Adopting Respondents’ rule would also risk overbroad spillover—inviting similar jurisdictional “reset” arguments after other forum-related interlocutory detours—contrary to the narrow-slice approach reflected in Griggs and ordinary equitable practice.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal district court that had original jurisdiction when it filed and then stayed an action pending arbitration under the FAA retains jurisdiction in that same case to decide post-arbitration motions (confirm/vacate/modify) without having to identify a new, independent jurisdictional basis.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Arbitration Act (FAA), 9 U.S.C. §§ 1–16 (especially §§ 9–10 concerning confirmation/vacatur and § 3 concerning stays), in interaction with federal subject-matter jurisdiction statutes (28 U.S.C. §§ 1331, 1332) and related jurisdiction doctrines (including principles reflected in 28 U.S.C. § 1367).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that once federal subject-matter jurisdiction properly exists at the outset (e.g., federal-question jurisdiction over Title VII/ADA/constitutional claims) and the district court stays—not dismisses—the case pending arbitration, the court keeps jurisdiction over the pending action and may rule on post-arbitration motions within that same case without requiring the moving party to plead a fresh, redundant basis for original jurisdiction; petitioner also contends the Second Circuit’s contrary rule is wrong, conflicts with other circuits (with substantial percolation), and creates unnecessary procedural traps and inefficiency.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that the Second Circuit’s decision does not warrant Supreme Court intervention (characterizing any split as weak/underdeveloped and the case as a poor vehicle) and that post-arbitration FAA motions require an independently sufficient jurisdictional basis rather than relying on the stayed action alone; they also contend alleged practical harms (forum-shopping/inefficiency) are overstated and that case-specific circumstances (including petitioner’s litigation positions/alternative arguments) complicate review.

Smarter Tools Inc. v. Chongqing SENCI Imp. & Exp. Trade Co., 57 F.4th 372 (2d Cir. 2023)
Weiss v. Sallie Mae, Inc., 939 F.3d 105 (2d Cir. 2019)
Triestman v. Fed. Bureau of Prisons, 470 F.3d 471 (2d Cir. 2006)
MasterCard (Second Circuit case cited in excerpt, 471 F.3d at 382–83)
Local Union No. 2 United Ass’n of Journeymen (Second Circuit case cited in excerpt, 841 F.2d 461 (2d Cir. 1988)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito presses the best counter: Badgerow and Kokkonen warn that the FAA supplies no jurisdiction and that case-management devices cannot create it. But that framing assumes the §§ 9–10 filing is a new, freestanding proceeding; as Justice Sotomayor and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 3 commands a stay of “the action,” which presupposes the same case remains pending on the court’s docket with its original, undisputed § 1331 jurisdiction intact. Nothing in §§ 9–10 clearly withdraws that existing jurisdiction or requires a second, redundant jurisdictional showing to seek post-award relief in the stayed case, and we should not treat statutory silence as jurisdiction-stripping. Badgerow is best confined to award-only proceedings initiated under the FAA, not to post-award motions filed in an already-properly-jurisdictioned action that Congress required the court to keep open.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s Badgerow/Kokkonen argument is the strongest counter, but it assumes the post-award motion is a new “application” that must independently reestablish jurisdiction even when filed in the same § 3–stayed action. As the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 3 commands the court to stay “the action” until arbitration is had; a stay preserves the pending case and the court’s already-invoked § 1331 or § 1332 jurisdiction unless Congress clearly withdraws it, which §§ 9–10 do not do. Badgerow addressed a freestanding award proceeding initiated under §§ 9–10 and rejected look-through as a basis to create jurisdiction in the first instance; it does not require us to treat a statutorily stayed federal case as jurisdictionally extinguished. Reading the FAA to impose a silent jurisdictional reset would convert § 3’s stay into a functional dismissal and would rest on jurisdiction-stripping by implication rather than text.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kagan press the strongest point: a §3 stay leaves the same “action” pending, so the court is merely continuing to exercise the §1331/§1332 jurisdiction it already had, not creating jurisdiction under the FAA. But that conflates continuing managerial authority over a stayed case with the distinct question whether Congress has supplied subject-matter jurisdiction to adjudicate the specific post-award “application” authorized by §§9–10—precisely the move Badgerow rejects when it requires an independent jurisdictional basis on the face of that application. Kokkonen reinforces that procedural mechanisms preserving a docket (or allowing a case to be reopened) do not themselves provide jurisdiction over a new claim for relief, and nothing in §3’s stay command “pegs” §§9–10 jurisdiction to the existence of a prior federal suit the way Congress sometimes does in other statutes. Absent a clear jurisdictional link in the FAA, treating the post-award request as simply “in-case” risks making a jurisdictional end-run around Badgerow’s statutory holding.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s Badgerow/Kokkonen argument is the best for Respondent, but it rests on a premise the text of §3 does not allow: that a post-award motion filed in the stayed docket is a jurisdictionally “new” proceeding. Section 3 commands the court “shall” stay “the action” “until such arbitration has been had,” and a stay’s ordinary legal effect is to keep the same action pending—not to terminate jurisdiction and require a fresh jurisdictional showing as if the case had been dismissed. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explain, Badgerow dealt with freestanding §§9–10 applications initiated as separate proceedings; nothing in §§9–10 purports to strip a district court of already-attached §1331/§1332 jurisdiction over an action Congress required it to keep on the docket. Treating §3’s mandatory stay as a nullity for jurisdictional purposes would evade the statute’s procedural design and convert a stay into dismissal-by-another-name without clear congressional command.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito is right to press Badgerow and Kokkonen: the FAA does not itself confer jurisdiction, and we cannot use a court’s managerial authority to invent it. But that point assumes the §§9–10 request is a new, freestanding “application” initiating a new proceeding; where, as the Chief Justice emphasizes, the district court had undisputed §1331 jurisdiction over an “action” and §3 required a stay of that same action “until such arbitration has been had,” the case remains pending and within the court’s continuing jurisdiction unless Congress clearly says otherwise. Nothing in §§9–10 withdraws or resets existing jurisdiction, and reading Badgerow to impose a second, redundant jurisdictional showing here would treat statutory silence as jurisdiction-stripping—the mirror-image error of the atextual jurisdiction-creation we rejected in Badgerow. So I would confine Badgerow to award-only proceedings commenced under §§9–10, while permitting post-award motions filed in the same stayed federal action to proceed on the court’s already-established jurisdiction.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s Badgerow/Kokkonen point is the sharpest: the FAA does not itself confer jurisdiction, and a court’s managerial acts cannot conjure it. But this case begins with undisputed §1331 jurisdiction over an “action,” and §3’s text commands the court to stay that same “action” pending arbitration—language that presupposes the case remains on the court’s docket and within its adjudicatory authority absent a clear statutory withdrawal. As the Chief Justice notes, Badgerow dealt with a freestanding §§9–10 proceeding initiated from scratch; it does not require us to treat a stayed federal-question case as silently extinguished for jurisdictional purposes when nothing in §§9–10 says so. Imposing a second, redundant jurisdictional prerequisite here would add an atextual hurdle—effectively converting Congress’s mandatory stay into a dismissal-by-another-name—without the clear congressional command our precedents demand.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s Badgerow/Kokkonen argument is the best for Respondent, but it treats a § 3 stay as if it silently terminates the court’s adjudicatory authority and forces a jurisdictional reset for a motion filed in the same pending case. As the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, the background principle of federal procedure is that a stay pauses proceedings without divesting jurisdiction, and nothing in §§ 9–10 clearly withdraws the district court’s already-secured § 1331 jurisdiction over the action Congress required it to keep on its docket. Badgerow’s independent-jurisdiction requirement fits freestanding FAA applications initiated from scratch; it does not compel recharacterizing an in-docket, case-linked post-award motion as a new civil action. Reading the FAA to demand refiling would functionally nullify § 3’s stay mechanism and create needless duplication and procedural traps inconsistent with the statute’s design.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s Badgerow/Kokkonen framing is the best pushback because it rightly insists that courts need an affirmative jurisdictional grant for the claim they are adjudicating, not merely “case-management” authority. But that objection assumes the §§ 9–11 motion is a freestanding proceeding; where the district court entered a mandatory § 3 stay, the same “action” remains pending on the court’s docket, and the court’s Article III jurisdiction—properly invoked under § 1331 or § 1332—continues absent a clear congressional withdrawal. As the Chief Justice notes, nothing in §§ 9–12 recharacterizes an in-docket post-award motion as a new civil action or strips jurisdiction already attached, and reading the FAA to require a jurisdictional reset would create a structural mismatch by treating the stayed federal action as ongoing for § 3 but jurisdictionally irrelevant for the award-related relief that resolves it. Badgerow is best confined, as Justice Kagan emphasizes, to award-only applications initiated under the FAA rather than motions that are incident to an already-jurisdictioned, still-pending federal case.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s Badgerow/Kokkonen argument is the best pushback because it correctly insists that the FAA does not itself confer jurisdiction and that courts cannot use case-management devices to manufacture it. But, as the Chief Justice and Justice Sotomayor emphasize, that framing misidentifies the jurisdictional posture: the district court already had undisputed § 1331 jurisdiction over a properly filed “action,” and § 3’s mandatory stay preserves that same action on the docket rather than converting later, case-linked motions into a new freestanding “application” that must independently reestablish jurisdiction. Nothing in §§ 9–11 clearly displaces the background rule that jurisdiction, once properly attached, continues through a stay and supports incidental proceedings necessary to resolve the pending action. Reading Badgerow to require a categorical jurisdictional reset here would treat statutory silence as jurisdiction-stripping and would destabilize ordinary post-stay federal practice in ways Congress did not clearly command.

John Roberts.reasoning: We have an independent obligation to assure jurisdiction, and here the district court indisputably had original federal-question jurisdiction over the filed action before entering a § 3 stay, leaving the case pending on the court’s docket rather than terminated. Properly read, Badgerow addresses the jurisdictional showing required for a freestanding §§ 9–10 “application” initiated as its own proceeding; it does not compel treating post-arbitration motions filed in the same stayed federal case as a new civil action requiring a second, redundant jurisdictional grant—doing so would recast a continuing case-management question as a subject-matter jurisdiction defect. The FAA’s text and structure support that distinction: § 3’s mandatory stay presupposes continued judicial supervision of the same action, and requiring a fresh jurisdictional basis after a stay would create a material and unnecessary change in posture (dismissal or state-court detour) despite the court’s ongoing jurisdiction over the underlying case. And to the extent jurisdictional and merits questions would become entangled (e.g., characterizing the post-arbitration filing as “new” versus “in-case” relief), we should not decide the merits of that characterization under the guise of jurisdiction where the case remained pending by statute-mandated stay.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The FAA’s text does not itself confer subject-matter jurisdiction for §§9–10 motions, see Badgerow, but this case begins with undisputed original federal-question jurisdiction and a §3 stay, which by its terms applies only to a “suit … pending” in the same court. A stay does not terminate the action; it preserves the court’s existing jurisdiction over that case, and nothing in §§9–10 affirmatively withdraws that jurisdiction or requires a second, freestanding jurisdictional showing for post-award relief sought in the same docket. Requiring a new jurisdictional basis effectively treats a stayed case as dismissed, contradicting §3’s structure and the background principle that jurisdiction, once properly invoked, continues unless Congress clearly provides otherwise. Because the district court retained the underlying Title VII/ADA case on its docket and merely stayed proceedings pending arbitration, it may resolve the ensuing confirm/vacate/modify motions as part of that same action without relitigating jurisdiction.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The antecedent question is not whether the district court may keep the stayed case on its docket, but whether it has subject-matter jurisdiction to decide a §§ 9–10 confirmation/vacatur application after arbitration ends. Under Badgerow, §§ 9–10 motions require an independent jurisdictional basis on the face of the application, and the fact that an earlier federal-question suit was filed and stayed under § 3 is a case-management fact that cannot itself supply jurisdiction over a new, statutorily authorized post-award proceeding. Kokkonen reinforces the distinction between a court’s procedural power to reopen or continue a case and the separate requirement of an affirmative jurisdictional grant; neither the FAA nor the existence of a stayed action creates federal jurisdiction absent § 1331 or § 1332 (or another statute) supporting the post-award application itself. Congress could have “pegged” §§ 9–10 jurisdiction to the existence of a stayed federal action but did not, and the service/notice provisions in §§ 9 and 12 read naturally as describing the mechanics of a distinct application rather than silently dispensing with jurisdictional requirements whenever an earlier suit happened to be stayed.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 3’s operative command is mandatory: the court “shall … stay the trial of the action until such arbitration has been had,” which by its ordinary legal meaning keeps the federal “action” pending rather than terminating it, leaving the court’s original subject-matter jurisdiction intact throughout the stay. Requiring a party, after arbitration concludes, to plead a new and independent jurisdictional basis to obtain confirmation or vacatur in the same stayed case effectively treats a stay as a dismissal, evading the text’s procedural design that preserves a return to federal court when arbitration ends or breaks down. Badgerow’s rule—that §§9–10 applications need an independent jurisdictional basis when they are freestanding proceedings—does not compel a contrary result where the court is acting within an already-filed, properly jurisdictioned action that Congress directed it to stay. Because Congress spoke in mandatory terms about maintaining the pending action “until” arbitration is had, appeals to judicially created jurisdictional obstacles cannot override that statutory architecture.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The district court had an independent jurisdictional basis at the outset (e.g., §1331 or §1332) and, by entering a §3 stay rather than dismissing, it kept the same civil action on its docket; the post-arbitration request to confirm/vacate is therefore a proceeding in that still-pending case, not a new FAA “action” demanding a second, freestanding jurisdictional showing. Nothing in §§9–10 purports to strip a court of jurisdiction it already properly has, and treating these motions as requiring a new jurisdictional grant would amount to an atextual restriction—just as impermissible as expanding jurisdiction without Congress’s say-so. Consistent with bedrock limits on jurisdiction, the key question is whether a statutory basis exists for federal power here; it does, because the court’s original jurisdiction continues through the stay and extends to ancillary/supplemental adjudication needed to resolve the case after arbitration. Requiring a redundant jurisdictional allegation would confuse the FAA’s “independent jurisdictional basis” rule (which prevents the FAA from creating jurisdiction in the first instance) with a rule that would negate jurisdiction already properly invoked.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The district court had undisputed original jurisdiction over petitioner’s federal-law claims when the action was filed, and § 3 of the FAA required the court to stay—rather than terminate—that same “action” pending arbitration; nothing in §§ 9–10 or elsewhere in the FAA says the court’s jurisdiction evaporates after the stay or that a party must plead a new, independent jurisdictional basis to seek relief in the still-pending case. Reading the statute as a whole, the post-arbitration motions are proceedings in the existing federal action the court has been commanded to pause, not a new standalone “civil action” demanding a fresh jurisdictional hook, and importing such a requirement would be a judge-made add-on inconsistent with text-first jurisdictional analysis. Badgerow addressed an award-only proceeding initiated under §§ 9–10 and rejected look-through jurisdiction there; it does not speak to (and cannot overcome) the continuing jurisdiction a court already possesses over a stayed federal-question case. This understanding accords with the Court’s statement that the “court with the power to stay the action under § 3 has the further power to confirm any ensuing arbitration award,” which fits the ordinary consequence of a stay: the court retains authority over the case it continues to hold on its docket.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: When the district court had undisputed original jurisdiction at the outset and then entered a § 3 stay (rather than a dismissal), the case remains on the court’s docket and within its continuing control; Congress legislated in the FAA against that clear background principle of ordinary federal procedure that a stayed action is still a pending action for purposes of later, case-related motions. Requiring a party to identify a new, independent jurisdictional basis for FAA §§ 9–11 relief in the very same stayed case would functionally nullify the stay mechanism Congress provided—forcing redundant filings and inviting procedural traps that waste resources and undermine arbitration’s promised efficiency. The Second Circuit’s contrary approach (as reflected in Beijing Shougang and related cases) treats the post-arbitration phase as jurisdictionally detached from the original, still-pending federal action, which is inconsistent with the structure of § 3 stays and mainstream procedural understanding. The sounder categorical rule is that, in a properly stayed federal case, the district court retains jurisdiction to resolve confirmation/vacatur/modification motions arising out of that arbitration without demanding a second jurisdictional showing.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The court’s power must be anchored in a valid jurisdictional grant, and here the district court indisputably had Article III subject-matter jurisdiction at the outset (federal-question claims) and kept the same “civil action” on its docket by entering a § 3 stay rather than a dismissal. In that posture, deciding a motion to confirm/vacate/modify the resulting award is best characterized not as invoking a new, freestanding original-jurisdiction proceeding under FAA §§ 9–11, but as an exercise of the court’s authority to adjudicate matters within the still-pending case; nothing in the FAA’s text withdraws that preexisting jurisdiction or requires a redundant re-pleading of § 1331/§ 1332. Reading the FAA to force a new, independent jurisdictional showing after a stay would create an interstatutory mismatch—treating the stayed federal action as both ongoing (for § 3) and jurisdictionally irrelevant (for §§ 9–11)—and would be hard to square with Congress’s decision to “lend the resources” of the district court to manage arbitration-related proceedings in the same case. Badgerow’s insistence on an independent jurisdictional basis for standalone enforcement petitions does not control because this is not a new action filed solely under the FAA, but a continuation of a properly filed federal case that the court never relinquished.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The relevant background rule is that once a federal court properly acquires subject-matter jurisdiction over a case, it retains authority to manage and resolve incidental, case-linked proceedings unless Congress clearly says otherwise; a § 3 stay keeps the action pending on the court’s docket rather than terminating it. Nothing in FAA §§ 9–11 or § 3 contains an express command that courts must identify a new, independent jurisdictional basis to decide post-arbitration confirm/vacate/modify motions when those motions are filed in the same stayed action that began with undisputed original jurisdiction, and Congress’s silence is not a basis to impose a categorical jurisdiction-stripping rule. Structural comparison reinforces that conclusion: where Congress wanted to dictate mandatory procedural consequences, it did so expressly (e.g., FAA § 3’s mandatory stay), so reading into §§ 9–11 a new jurisdictional “re-filing” requirement is an atextual overlay that would destabilize ordinary federal practice. Limiting Badgerow to freestanding, post-arbitration petitions also avoids an overbroad logic that would unsettle other routine post-stay/post-appeal proceedings and create needless procedural traps in cases that never left federal court.
